practice_questions.text:
Which method of heat transfer involves the movement of circulating currents within a liquid?
A. Conduction
B. Convection
C. Radiation
D. Evaporation
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for B. Convection.

practice_questions.text: Name two reasons why food is cooked.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each valid reason (any two from): make food safe to eat; develop flavours; improve texture; improve shelf life; give variety in the diet.

practice_questions.text: Describe how heat is transferred to food when it is placed under a grill.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: identification of radiation as the mechanism (1); explanation that the grill element emits infrared waves (1); statement that infrared travels without a medium and heats the surface of the food directly (1). Credit also: the surface browns/chars rapidly because radiation acts directly on the food surface (1) in place of any of the above.

practice_questions.text: Priya is making a beef stew for her family. She decides to braise the beef in stock on the hob rather than dry-roasting it in the oven. Explain why braising in liquid might be a better choice for preserving the tenderness of the beef.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: braising uses a water-based method where the beef is partially submerged in liquid (1); convection currents in the hot stock circulate heat around the meat gently and evenly (1); the low, sustained temperature over a long time breaks down the tough collagen in the beef into gelatine, making it tender (1); dry-roasting uses higher temperatures and dry heat, which can tighten (coagulate) the protein fibres and make the meat tough if overcooked (1).

practice_questions.text:
Luca is a year 10 student preparing a vegetable stir-fry and a vegetable soup as two dishes for a cookery assessment. He is thinking about which cooking method best preserves the vitamin C content of his broccoli and red pepper.

Explain how the choice of cooking method affects the vitamin C content of vegetables, and recommend which method Luca should use for maximum retention of vitamin C. Give reasons for your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Clear identification that vitamin C is water-soluble and leaches into cooking water; developed explanation of why boiling/simmering causes significant vitamin C loss (long contact with water, heat); clear explanation of why stir-frying retains more vitamin C (very high heat for a short time, no water, food moves quickly through the pan); recommendation of stir-fry with a supported reason; accurate use of food-science vocabulary (water-soluble, leach, denaturation of cell walls); applied to Luca's specific dishes.
Secure (3-4 marks): Correct identification that boiling causes vitamin C loss; some explanation of why; recommendation made but reasoning is partial or not fully linked to Luca's context.
Developing (2 marks): Relevant points about cooking affecting vitamins but limited development; may state stir-frying is better without explaining why.
Emerging (1 mark): Basic point such as 'boiling destroys vitamins' with no further explanation.

practice_questions.text: State two ways in which marinating meat in an acid-based marinade changes the meat before it is cooked.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each valid point (any two from): the acid denatures the protein in the surface layer, unfolding the protein chains; the texture of the meat softens/tenderises; flavours from the marinade penetrate more deeply into the meat; moisture from the marinade is absorbed, keeping the meat juicier during cooking.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the correct description of Physical Activity Level (PAL)?
A) The minimum energy needed by the body at rest
B) A multiplier applied to BMR to calculate total daily energy requirement
C) The recommended daily intake of carbohydrates for an active person
D) The percentage of energy that should come from fat
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for B.

practice_questions.text: State two factors, other than cost, that could influence a person's food choice.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of any two valid factors from: physical activity level (PAL), food availability, celebration/occasion, preferences, enjoyment, income, healthy eating, lifestyles, seasonality, time of day, time available to prepare/cook. Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe how seasonality can affect the food choices made by a family when planning their weekly meals.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: identification of what seasonality means (1); description of how it affects availability of specific foods or their price (1); link to how this shapes a family's meal choices, e.g. root vegetable stews in winter, lighter salads in summer (1).

practice_questions.text: Callum is 16 and plays rugby for his school team three times a week. He is planning his weekday meals for the coming term. Explain two reasons why Callum's food choices might be different from those of a classmate who does not play sport.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks per reason (2 reasons required). Reason 1: Callum has a higher physical activity level (PAL), which means his total energy requirement is greater; as a result he may choose larger portions or more energy-dense foods such as starchy carbohydrates (1 + 1). Reason 2: his higher muscle-repair needs mean he may prioritise protein-rich foods such as chicken, eggs or dairy, because these supply essential amino acids needed for growth and recovery after training (1 + 1). Other valid explained reasons acceptable (time constraints from training schedule; greater appetite driving larger portion sizes).

practice_questions.text: A recipe for a vegetable curry costs £3.20 in total and serves 4 people. The cook wants to make a modified version that feeds 6 people. She adds an extra 200 g of tinned chickpeas (£0.45 per tin of 400 g) and an extra 150 g of spinach (£0.80 per 200 g bag). Calculate the new cost per portion for the modified recipe serving 6.
practice_questions.marks: Cost of extra chickpeas: 200 g from a 400 g tin at £0.45 = £0.225 (round to £0.23) (1). Cost of extra spinach: 150 g from a 200 g bag at £0.80 = £0.60 (1). New total = £3.20 + £0.23 + £0.60 = £4.03. Cost per portion = £4.03 ÷ 6 = £0.67 (accept £0.67–£0.68). Full credit for correct working shown even if minor rounding differs.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which cost and income are the most important factors influencing the food choices of a family of four living on a limited budget in a British city. In your answer, consider other factors that also affect their choices.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12): sustained evaluation of cost and income as primary drivers (e.g. food poverty restricts access to fresh produce; unit pricing and special offers dominate purchasing decisions; cheap, energy-dense foods chosen over nutritionally diverse options because of affordability). Considers at least two other significant factors (e.g. time available — a working parent with childcare responsibilities has little time to cook from scratch; seasonality — seasonal produce is cheaper and more accessible; lifestyle and habits — preferences formed in childhood persist regardless of income). Reaches a supported judgement: cost and income are highly significant but interact with time and availability; removing financial barriers alone may not change habits without also addressing time and cooking confidence. Uses precise terminology (food poverty, PAL, recipe costing, food availability, seasonality). Applied throughout to a named family context.

Secure (7–9): addresses cost and income with reasonable development; considers at least one other factor with some development; reaches a partial judgement but weighing of evidence is limited.

Developing (4–6): describes cost and possibly one other factor; limited application to the specified family; no clear judgement reached.

Emerging (1–3): simple points about cost or food choice with no development or judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a high-risk food?
A. Dried pasta
B. Cooked chicken left at room temperature
C. Wholegrain bread in a sealed bag
D. Unprocessed oats
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for B (cooked chicken left at room temperature). Dried pasta, sealed bread and unprocessed oats all have low water activity or will be cooked before eating; cooked chicken is moist, high in protein, and ready-to-eat — a classic high-risk food.

practice_questions.text: State two conditions that microorganisms need in order to multiply rapidly.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct condition, up to 2 marks. Accept any two from: food/nutrients; moisture/water availability; warmth/temperature (within the danger zone, 5–63°C); time. Do not accept vague answers such as 'the right environment' without specifics.

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens during enzymic browning when a potato is peeled and left in the air.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: (1) enzymes in the potato (polyphenol oxidases) are exposed when cells are cut/damaged; (1) the enzymes react with oxygen in the air; (1) this produces brown pigments, discolouring the surface of the potato. A response that names the enzyme type and its substrate is not required at GCSE but would be credited if accurate.

practice_questions.text: Priya is making a fruit salad for a school event. She prepares it two hours before serving and notices the apple and pear slices have turned brown. Explain two methods Priya could have used to prevent this discolouration, and why each method works.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct method + 1 mark for the linked explanation, up to 4 marks total. Method 1: Add an acid such as lemon juice — because the low pH deactivates/denatures the browning enzymes so they cannot react with oxygen. Method 2: Cover/wrap the cut fruit tightly in cling film or place in water — because limiting contact with oxygen prevents the enzymic oxidation reaction. Other accepted methods: refrigerating the fruit (cold temperature slows enzyme activity); soaking in acidulated water. Each method must be paired with a 'because' explanation to gain both marks.

practice_questions.text: A small community bakery uses both yeast and a Penicillium mould culture in its production. Explain, with named examples, how each of these microorganisms is used beneficially in food production.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Two or three well-developed points for each microorganism, with accurate use of food-science vocabulary. Yeast explanation covers: feeds on sugars in dough; produces CO2 gas; gas is trapped by gluten network; dough rises during proving; alcohol evaporates during baking. Mould explanation covers: Penicillium introduced into cheese such as Stilton or Roquefort; breaks down proteins and fats; creates characteristic blue-green veins and strong tangy flavour; controlled by temperature and moisture during maturation. Correct named examples given for both.

Secure (3–4 marks): Both microorganisms addressed with some accurate science and at least one named example. Development is partial — may describe the process without fully explaining the mechanism.

Developing (2 marks): One microorganism addressed with some accuracy, or both addressed at a basic level with limited development. Limited use of technical vocabulary.

Emerging (1 mark): Basic statement about one use with little or no explanation (e.g. 'yeast makes bread rise').

practice_questions.text: Name the three signs of food spoilage recognised in food science.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for naming all three correctly: enzymic action (or enzymic browning), mould growth, yeast action. All three must be named for the mark. Partial credit is not awarded for this question.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes intensive farming?
A. Animals are given outdoor access and space to roam freely.
B. Large numbers of animals are kept indoors in confined conditions to maximise output.
C. Crops are grown without the use of synthetic pesticides or fertilisers.
D. Fish are caught at a rate that allows populations to replenish naturally.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for B.

practice_questions.text: Give two disadvantages of free-range production compared with intensive farming.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of two acceptable disadvantages from: higher cost to produce/purchase; lower output per unit of land; less efficient use of space; smaller quantities produced; not accessible to all consumers on low incomes. Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by sustainable fishing.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: definition of sustainable fishing as harvesting fish at a rate that allows populations to replenish (1); reference to protecting long-term fish stocks or preventing over-fishing (1); example such as MSC certification, fish farming/aquaculture, or catch quotas as a method used to achieve sustainability (1).

practice_questions.text: Priya runs a small village farm shop. She sells locally grown seasonal vegetables alongside nationally distributed imported produce. Explain why buying locally grown seasonal vegetables could benefit both the environment and the consumer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Environmental benefit with reason (2): e.g. local food travels fewer miles, so less carbon dioxide is produced in transportation, reducing the farm’s carbon footprint (up to 2 marks for a developed explanation); seasonal produce does not need energy-intensive glasshouse growing or refrigerated long-haul transport. Consumer benefit with reason (2): e.g. seasonal produce is at peak freshness and flavour because it has not been stored or transported long distances; it may be cheaper when in-season surplus drives prices down. Two developed explanations required for full marks.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using genetically modified (GM) crops as a way of addressing food production challenges.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–9): Identifies and develops multiple advantages and disadvantages of GM crops with accurate scientific and social reasoning. Advantages discussed with development: pest resistance reduces pesticide use; drought tolerance allows crops to survive water stress; higher yields from less land; potential to address food shortages in regions with poor growing conditions. Disadvantages discussed with development: unknown long-term health effects on consumers; risk of harm to non-target organisms such as beneficial insects; biodiversity concerns if GM crops cross-pollinate wild relatives; concentration of seed supply in a small number of corporations limiting farmer independence; public distrust reducing uptake. Considers multiple dimensions (environmental, economic, health, social) and examines relationships between them. Accurate use of terminology throughout.

Secure (5–6): Identifies advantages and disadvantages with some development of each. Generally accurate. Links points to food production challenges but reasoning may be partial.

Developing (3–4): Identifies some advantages and some disadvantages but with limited development. May be one-sided. Points stated without clear “because” reasoning.

Emerging (1–2): Basic points about GM foods. Little or no development or application to food production challenges. May list pros and cons without any explanation.

practice_questions.text: A school canteen is reviewing its meat purchasing policy. Compare organic and conventionally farmed meat, giving one advantage and one disadvantage of each.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks. Organic advantage (1): e.g. no synthetic pesticides/antibiotics used in production; better animal welfare standards typically applied; may appeal to ethically minded students. Organic disadvantage (1): higher cost per kilogram making large-scale school catering expensive. Conventional advantage (1): lower cost per kilogram; widely available in bulk for catering. Conventional disadvantage (1): may use synthetic pesticides or antibiotics; lower animal welfare standards in some operations. Any three distinct points with correct attribution to the correct farming type. Maximum 3 marks.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following foods is a source of high biological value (HBV) protein?
A. Brown rice
B. Kidney beans
C. Lentils
D. Eggs
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for D (Eggs). Rice, kidney beans and lentils are all LBV protein sources.

practice_questions.text: State two protein alternatives suitable for a vegan diet.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: TVP (textured vegetable protein); soya; mycoprotein (Quorn); tofu. Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by protein complementation and give one example of how it is used in a meal.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that protein complementation means combining two or more LBV protein sources; 1 mark for explaining that this supplies all essential amino acids that would be missing from one source alone; 1 mark for a named example (e.g. beans on toast / rice and peas / lentil soup with bread / hummus and pitta). Up to 3 marks.

practice_questions.text: Priya is 15 and has recently become vegan. Her parents are concerned she may not be getting enough protein. Explain two steps Priya could take to meet her protein needs on a vegan diet.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 2 marks available per developed explanation (1 for the point, 1 for the developed reason or consequence). Examples: (1) Use protein complementation — combining two LBV sources such as beans on toast, because together they supply all nine essential amino acids that a single LBV source is missing. (2) Include soya products (tofu, edamame, soya milk) because soya is the only naturally HBV plant protein and will supply all essential amino acids without needing complementation. (3) Use mycoprotein or TVP as meat substitutes, because these are manufactured to have a comparable amino acid profile to meat and supply adequate protein. 1 mark for identification; 1 mark for developed reasoning, per point.

practice_questions.text: Describe the health effects of consuming a diet high in saturated fat over a long period of time.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks. 1 mark for identifying that saturated fat raises LDL (bad) cholesterol; 1 mark for explaining that raised LDL causes narrowing/blocking of arteries (atherosclerosis); 1 mark for linking this to an increased risk of coronary heart disease (CHD) or stroke/heart attack. Award marks for any three accurate, distinct points.

practice_questions.text: Caitlin is a food technology teacher. She is planning a lesson to show students how to adapt a traditional beef lasagne recipe for a vegan family. Explain how Caitlin could adapt the protein sources in the lasagne while ensuring the dish still provides adequate protein for growth and repair in the teenage students who will eat it.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Identifies at least two protein substitutes (e.g. TVP or lentils for mince; cashew or soya-based cheese for dairy cheese) and explains how each works in the dish and why it provides adequate protein (TVP absorbs the tomato sauce flavour and supplies a protein profile similar to meat once fortified; lentils are LBV but when combined with wheat pasta achieve complementation; soya-based cheese is HBV). Sustained application to the teenage growth context (growth requires adequate essential amino acid supply for muscle and tissue repair). Accurate use of HBV/LBV/complementation vocabulary throughout.

Secure (3–4 marks): Identifies at least one substitute with development, or two substitutes with limited development. Some reference to adequate protein or growth context. Mostly accurate.

Developing (2 marks): Names a substitute without explaining how it provides adequate protein, or gives a general statement about vegan diets being low in protein without applying it to the lasagne scenario.

Emerging (1 mark): Very basic or partially relevant response, e.g. 'use tofu instead of meat' with no development or nutritional reasoning.

practice_questions.text:
Which vitamin is produced in the skin when exposed to sunlight and is essential for calcium absorption?
A. Vitamin A
B. Vitamin C
C. Vitamin D
D. Vitamin K
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for C (Vitamin D).

practice_questions.text: Give two reasons why water-soluble vitamins are often lost when vegetables are boiled.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: the vitamins dissolve into the cooking water; the vitamins are destroyed/broken down by heat; the longer the cooking time, the greater the loss. Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe the functions of vitamin C in the body and identify two good dietary sources.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of any three distinct points from: needed for collagen synthesis (skin, blood vessels, wound healing); supports immune function; acts as an antioxidant (neutralises free radicals/protects cells from damage); increases absorption of non-haem iron from plant foods. Plus 1 mark each for two named sources (e.g. oranges, kiwi, strawberries, peppers, broccoli, potatoes). Up to 3 marks total — any three distinct points from functions and sources combined.

practice_questions.text: Theo is a 16-year-old vegetarian who rarely eats dairy products. His GP has raised concerns about his vitamin D and calcium intake. Explain why Theo is at risk and suggest two ways he could improve his intake of both nutrients.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 2 marks available per developed point. (1) Vitamin D: Theo is at risk because dairy (milk, yoghurt, cheese) is a key dietary source of vitamin D; without it, absorption of calcium will also be reduced because vitamin D is needed for calcium uptake. He could improve intake by spending time outdoors (sunlight triggers skin synthesis of vitamin D) or eating fortified foods such as plant milks and fortified cereals. (2) Calcium: without dairy, major sources of calcium are removed from his diet; deficiency can lead to poor bone density and increased risk of osteoporosis. He could eat canned fish with bones (sardines), dark green leafy vegetables (kale, broccoli), or fortified plant milks. 1 mark for identification of risk; 1 mark for developed explanation or practical solution per point.

practice_questions.text: Name two antioxidant vitamins and describe how antioxidants protect body cells.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of two correctly named antioxidant vitamins (Vitamin A / Vitamin C / Vitamin E — any two); 1 mark for explaining that antioxidants neutralise free radicals (unstable molecules) which would otherwise damage cell membranes and DNA. Up to 3 marks.

practice_questions.text: Sienna is a student nurse who wants to plan a week of packed lunches that preserve water-soluble vitamins as much as possible. She often prepares lunches the evening before and takes vegetables raw or cooked. Explain how Sienna should prepare, store and choose her food to maximise water-soluble vitamin content, linking your answer to the chemistry of vitamin loss.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Explains at least two mechanisms of vitamin loss (dissolving into cooking water; destroyed by heat; oxidation when cut surfaces are exposed to air) and links each to a specific practical strategy (steam or stir-fry rather than boil; prepare vegetables just before eating rather than overnight; store in a sealed container in a cool place to minimise oxidation; include raw salad vegetables such as peppers and tomatoes; choose vitamin-C-rich foods that can be eaten raw). Accurately identifies B-group and vitamin C as the affected vitamins. Sustained, well-developed reasoning chains using correct terminology.

Secure (3–4 marks): Identifies at least one mechanism and two practical strategies. Generally accurate. Some development of reasoning.

Developing (2 marks): Names water-soluble vitamins and suggests a practical tip but without explaining the underlying reason, or gives a general statement about cooking destroying vitamins without specifying which ones or how.

Emerging (1 mark): Very limited response, e.g. 'cook vegetables quickly' with no explanation.

practice_questions.text:
What does the term 'food miles' measure?
A. The nutritional value of food per kilogram
B. The distance food travels from production to the consumer
C. The weight of packaging used to transport food
D. The number of countries a food product passes through
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for B.

practice_questions.text: State two environmental problems caused by excessive food packaging.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of two acceptable problems from: plastic waste in landfill or water systems; non-biodegradable materials taking hundreds of years to break down; increased transport weight requiring more fuel; contribution to greenhouse gas emissions during manufacture; litter and wildlife harm. Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe three challenges to global food security.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of three distinct challenges described with relevant detail: climate change/global warming disrupting growing seasons (1); drought and flooding destroying crops (1); growing global population increasing demand on finite farmland (1); insufficient or degraded land for growing food (1); food waste reducing available supply (1). Any three, each with sufficient description. Maximum 3 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Fairtrade supports food security and sustainable livelihoods for farmers in developing countries.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Guarantee of a minimum fair price (1) because it protects farmers from price volatility in global markets, meaning they have stable income to invest in their farms (1). Fairtrade premium funds community infrastructure such as schools, healthcare and clean water (1) which improves living conditions and enables communities to sustain agricultural production long-term (1). Two developed explanations linking the mechanism to the consequence required for full marks.

practice_questions.text: A secondary school is developing a sustainability policy for its canteen. The canteen currently sources most ingredients from a large national distributor, uses significant single-use plastic packaging, and throws away a substantial amount of prepared food each day. Analyse the environmental impact of the canteen's current food practices and suggest how each could be improved.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–9): Identifies all three issues (sourcing, packaging, waste) and analyses each with a developed chain of environmental consequences. Sourcing: national distributor means high food miles and associated carbon dioxide emissions; switching to local/seasonal suppliers reduces transport emissions and supports local economy. Packaging: single-use plastic contributes to landfill, water pollution and slow breakdown; switching to recyclable or biodegradable materials and reducing portion sizes of packaging reduces environmental harm. Waste: daily prepared food waste produces methane in landfill and wastes the energy/water used in production; solutions include better demand forecasting, smaller batch cooking, donating near-date food, composting unavoidable waste. Analysis examines relationships between the issues (e.g. better sourcing also reduces packaging needs) and evaluates the practical feasibility of solutions. Accurate use of terminology (food miles, carbon footprint, food waste, sustainability) throughout.

Secure (5–6): Addresses at least two issues with developed analysis. Generally accurate. Links issues to environmental consequences. Solutions present but may be limited.

Developing (3–4): Identifies issues with limited development. One-sided or descriptive. Points stated without clear consequence chain.

Emerging (1–2): Basic identification of one or two issues. Little or no environmental analysis. Vague suggestions.

practice_questions.text: Name one specific strategy a household could use to reduce food waste at home.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: meal planning before shopping; correct food storage (fridge/freezer temperatures); freezing food before use-by date; using leftovers creatively; buying only what is needed; checking use-by and best-before dates when shopping.

practice_questions.text:
Which food-poisoning bacterium can grow at refrigerator temperatures and is especially dangerous for pregnant women?
A. Campylobacter
B. Salmonella
C. Listeria
D. Staphylococcus aureus
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for C (Listeria). Campylobacter and salmonella are destroyed by thorough cooking and do not grow well at fridge temperatures. Staphylococcus aureus produces heat-resistant toxins but does not grow well at fridge temperatures.

practice_questions.text: Name two food-poisoning bacteria and give one typical source for each.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct bacterium-source pair, up to 2 marks. Accept any two from: campylobacter — raw/undercooked poultry; e-coli — undercooked minced beef or contaminated water or raw vegetables; salmonella — raw poultry or raw eggs; listeria — soft mould-ripened cheeses, cold deli meats, smoked fish; staphylococcus aureus — food handlers' skin/nose/throat or cooked foods at room temperature. The bacterium and source must be correctly matched for the mark.

practice_questions.text: Describe three symptoms of bacterial food poisoning.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correctly described symptom, up to 3 marks. Accept: nausea; vomiting; diarrhoea; stomach cramps/abdominal pain; fever/raised temperature; headache; general malaise. Answers must describe the symptom, not just name it — e.g. 'raised body temperature' is better than just 'fever' but both are acceptable for 1 mark each.

practice_questions.text: Omar is a food handler at a school canteen. He has a small cut on his finger and has been preparing egg mayonnaise sandwiches. Explain why this situation poses a food safety risk and how Omar should address it.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the specific risk (staphylococcus aureus on skin/in wounds); 1 mark for explaining the mechanism (bacteria transfers from cut to food during handling); 1 mark for correct control method (cover cut with a blue waterproof plaster); 1 mark for a second linked explanation or additional control (wash hands thoroughly before handling food; egg mayonnaise is a high-risk chilled food that must be kept below 5°C to slow bacterial growth). Must use linking language ('because' or 'this means that') for the explanation marks.

practice_questions.text: Assess the food safety risks associated with preparing and serving a chicken dish at a community cookery event. In your answer, refer to sources of contamination, the bacteria involved, and how the risks can be controlled.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): Thorough analysis breaking the preparation and serving process into distinct stages: buying/storage (campylobacter on raw chicken; refrigerate at 0–5°C; keep separate from ready-to-eat foods); preparation (cross-contamination from board/knife to other foods; wash hands; use separate colour-coded boards); cooking (must reach 75°C throughout to destroy campylobacter and salmonella; use a temperature probe); serving and holding (keep above 63°C or below 5°C; time in danger zone; staphylococcus aureus risk if food handlers have skin infections). Names at least three bacteria with their specific sources and controls. Examines consequences (not just lists risks) — e.g. links campylobacter survival to undercooking, links staphylococcus aureus toxin heat-stability to the importance of preventing contamination in the first place. Sustained application to the community event context throughout.

Secure (5–7 marks): Most stages of the process addressed; at least two bacteria named with sources; controls given but some links between risk and consequence are missing. Context applied but not consistently.

Developing (3–4 marks): Some relevant risks identified; one or two bacteria named; controls listed without full explanation of why they work. Limited application to the event context.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic food safety points (cook thoroughly, wash hands) with little or no bacterium-specific knowledge or reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Identify the food-poisoning bacterium whose toxins remain dangerous even after the contaminated food is reheated.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for staphylococcus aureus. Accept 'staph aureus' or 'S. aureus' but not just 'staph' without the genus context.

practice_questions.text: Name the food principle followed by Muslims that governs how animals are slaughtered and which foods are permitted.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: halal (accept Halal).

practice_questions.text: State two food restrictions followed by observant Jews when keeping a Kosher diet.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of any two valid points: pork and pork products are forbidden; shellfish are forbidden; meat and dairy must not be eaten together / must be prepared on separate surfaces with separate utensils; animals must be slaughtered by a trained shochet using the correct method. Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between a food intolerance and a food allergy, using one example of each.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: food intolerance is a non-immune digestive reaction causing uncomfortable but usually non-life-threatening symptoms (1); a food allergy is an immune-system reaction that can be life-threatening (anaphylaxis) (1); valid example of intolerance such as lactose intolerance causing bloating (1) or valid example of allergy such as nut allergy causing anaphylaxis (1). Maximum 3 marks.

practice_questions.text: Sanjay is preparing a birthday dinner for his Hindu grandparents who are strict vegetarians and do not eat beef or pork. He wants to serve a spaghetti bolognese. Explain two modifications he should make to the recipe, giving a reason for each change.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks per modification (2 required). Modification 1: replace beef mince with a plant-based alternative such as lentils, Quorn, soya mince or mushrooms (1); because beef is avoided by most Hindus as the cow is considered sacred, and plant-based proteins are suitable for vegetarians (1). Modification 2: check the pasta does not contain egg (some fresh pasta does) or use a certified egg-free dried pasta (1); because some strict vegetarians also avoid eggs depending on their interpretation (1). Other valid modifications accepted: replace any meat stock with vegetable stock; ensure any cheese used is vegetarian rennet; justify clearly each time.

practice_questions.text: A school is planning a whole-school celebration lunch that must be suitable for students of all religious and cultural backgrounds represented in the school, including Muslims, Jews, Hindus and Rastafari. Explain how the caterer could plan the menu to meet these requirements.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): clearly explains why each religious group's requirements affect specific dishes; identifies overlapping restrictions (e.g. no pork satisfies multiple groups; a fully vegetarian menu using plant proteins satisfies all); explains specific substitutions with reasons (e.g. halal-certified meat satisfies Muslim students; plant-based dishes with Ital-style fresh herbs satisfy Rastafari principles; no meat-and-dairy combinations in the same dish respects Kosher principles; vegetarian options satisfy Hindu and many Buddhist students); considers label transparency and allergen marking. Two or three well-developed reasoning chains using accurate vocabulary.

Secure (3–4): addresses most religious groups with some development; mostly accurate; some application to the practical catering scenario.

Developing (1–2): names some restrictions with little explanation or development; limited application to menu planning.

Emerging (0): superficial points only; no religious requirements correctly identified.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how ethical and moral beliefs such as animal welfare, Fairtrade and views on GM foods can influence food purchasing decisions, using examples throughout your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9): breaks ethical food choice into distinct components; animal welfare (1) — link between intensive farming and low price vs welfare certification and premium cost; consumer may pay more for free-range eggs or outdoor-reared pork because they value reduced animal suffering, which means demand for cheap intensively farmed products falls among ethically motivated consumers (2). Fairtrade — farmers in developing countries receive guaranteed floor price; consumer choice to buy Fairtrade coffee funds community development but typically costs more; analyses the trade-off between personal cost and global justice (2). GM foods — opposition linked to uncertainty about long-term health effects or environmental concern (superweeds, monoculture risk); support linked to yield increases that reduce food prices or can address food insecurity; analyses both sides (2). Examines how these beliefs interact with income (ethical choices often more expensive; affluent consumers more able to act on values). Accurate vocabulary throughout.

Secure (5–7): addresses at least two ethical areas with reasonable development and some analysis of relationships and consequences.

Developing (2–4): describes ethical factors with limited analysis; one-sided or descriptive.

Emerging (1): lists terms with no development.

practice_questions.text:
Which term describes the process in which denatured protein chains bond together and solidify on continued heating?
A. Gelatinisation
B. Dextrinisation
C. Coagulation
D. Foam formation
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for C. Coagulation.

practice_questions.text: Name the two proteins in wheat flour that combine to form gluten when water is added.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for glutenin; 1 mark for gliadin.

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens to starch granules during gelatinisation.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: the starch granules absorb liquid and begin to swell as temperature rises above approximately 60 degrees C (1); above approximately 85 degrees C the granules burst, releasing starch molecules into the liquid (1); the released starch molecules tangle together and thicken the mixture into a gel (1).

practice_questions.text: Niamh is making shortcrust pastry for a quiche. Her teacher tells her the pastry should be handled as little as possible. Explain why over-working the pastry dough would make the finished result tough rather than crumbly.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: wheat flour contains two proteins, glutenin and gliadin (1); when water is added and the dough is worked, these combine to form gluten (1); the more the dough is kneaded or worked, the stronger and more elastic the gluten network becomes (1); a strong gluten network makes the pastry tough and chewy rather than short and crumbly, because the protein strands have bonded extensively and resist breaking apart (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the functional properties of both starch and egg protein work together to produce a smooth, set quiche filling, and explain what happens when the quiche is overbaked.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8-9 marks): Accurate identification and explanation of gelatinisation (starch from any flour or thickener in the filling absorbs liquid and helps create a smooth gel texture) and protein coagulation (egg protein denatures then coagulates when heated, setting the custard filling); clear analysis of how these two processes work together (the starch and egg protein both contribute to structure, each playing a different role); clear analysis of the effect of overbaking (over-coagulation causes protein network to contract, expelling water, giving rubbery, watery, shrunken filling; also over-heating starch can break down the gel structure); accurate food-science vocabulary throughout; sustained reasoning linking cause to effect.
Secure (5-7 marks): Correct identification of both gelatinisation and coagulation with some explanation; some analysis of overbaking effects; vocabulary mostly accurate; some but not full examination of the relationships between the two processes.
Developing (3-4 marks): One of the two processes well-described; some mention of the other; limited analysis of overbaking or only descriptive.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic relevant points only, e.g. 'egg sets on heating' with no further development.

practice_questions.text: State two differences between dextrinisation and caramelisation.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each valid difference (any two from): dextrinisation involves starch; caramelisation involves sugars; dextrinisation occurs above approximately 110 degrees C, caramelisation above approximately 160 degrees C (so caramelisation needs a higher temperature); dextrinisation produces a toasted/bread crust flavour, caramelisation produces a sweet/nutty/bitter caramel flavour; examples: dextrinisation gives bread its brown crust; caramelisation gives creme brulee its glassy top or roasted vegetables their sweet surface.

practice_questions.text:
What is the correct temperature for a domestic freezer, according to Food Standards Agency guidelines?
A. 0°C
B. −5°C
C. −18°C
D. −25°C
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for C (−18°C). 0°C is the lower limit for chilling, not freezing. −5°C and −25°C are not the FSA-specified freezer temperature.

practice_questions.text: State the difference between a 'use by' date and a 'best before' date on food packaging.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct statement, up to 2 marks. 'Use by' — a food safety date; eating after this date poses a health risk; applies to perishable high-risk foods. 'Best before' — a quality date; food may decline in flavour, texture or nutritional value after this date but is not necessarily unsafe; applies to lower-risk ambient foods such as tinned goods or dried pasta. Both distinctions must be present for both marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe three personal hygiene practices a food handler should follow when preparing a chicken stir-fry.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correctly described practice, up to 3 marks. Accept: wash hands thoroughly with soap and warm water before handling food; wash hands after handling raw chicken before touching other ingredients; cover any cuts with a blue waterproof plaster; tie back hair/wear a hair covering; avoid touching the face, nose or mouth during preparation; wear clean clothing. Answers must describe the practice, not just state a vague rule.

practice_questions.text: Theo is a trainee chef who cooks a whole roast chicken. The skin looks golden and the juices run clear, but when he inserts a temperature probe into the thickest part of the breast, the reading shows 68°C. Explain the action Theo should take and why it is necessary.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct action (return the chicken to the oven / continue cooking); 1 mark for explanation of why (the internal temperature has not yet reached 75°C, so harmful bacteria — such as campylobacter or salmonella — may not have been destroyed); 1 mark for explaining why visual checks alone are insufficient (surface appearance can look cooked while the centre remains below 75°C); 1 mark for reference to the role of the probe (the probe measures internal temperature, which is the only reliable indicator of safety). Must use linking language for the explanation marks.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate how effectively a home cook could manage the food safety risks when preparing, cooking and serving a buffet of cooked chicken, egg mayonnaise and prawn cocktail for a family celebration.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): Comprehensive coverage of buying and storage risks (temperature control, raw-cooked separation, correct fridge shelf placement), preparation risks (cross-contamination from raw poultry via hands and equipment; campylobacter and salmonella; colour-coded boards; handwashing), cooking risks (chicken must reach 75°C throughout; use of a temperature probe; not relying on visual checks alone), and serving/holding risks (all three dishes — chicken, egg mayo and prawn cocktail — are high-risk chilled foods that must stay below 5°C on the buffet; time in danger zone; staphylococcus aureus risk from food handlers). Evaluates the feasibility of home cooks managing all risks consistently (lacks commercial equipment, training, probes; emotional distraction at a celebration). Reaches a supported judgement with weighing — e.g. which risk factor is hardest to control in a domestic setting and why. Uses accurate technical vocabulary throughout.

Secure (7–9 marks): Most stages addressed; at least three bacteria or contamination routes named with correct controls; some evaluation of difficulty/effectiveness rather than just listing rules; judgement present but may not be fully supported.

Developing (4–6 marks): Relevant safety points listed but mostly as rules without evaluation; one or two bacteria named; controls given; little or no assessment of how effectively a home cook could manage all risks; no clear judgement or judgement unsupported.

Emerging (1–3 marks): Basic rules listed (cook thoroughly, wash hands, keep food cold) with little or no bacterial knowledge, no evaluation, and no judgement.

practice_questions.text: Give the temperature of the food temperature danger zone.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the lower boundary (5°C); 1 mark for the upper boundary (63°C). Both must be correct and must be stated as a range (e.g. '5°C to 63°C') for 2 marks. Accepting each boundary independently: 1 mark for 5°C alone; 1 mark for 63°C alone. Vague answers such as 'room temperature' or 'between cold and hot' score 0.

practice_questions.text: Name the five food groups shown in the Eatwell Guide.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for all five named correctly: fruit and vegetables; starchy carbohydrates; dairy and dairy alternatives; protein foods (beans, pulses, fish, eggs, meat and alternatives); oils and spreads. Accept a clearly correct description of any five distinct groups. (1 mark for all five; do not award for a partial list of fewer than four.)

practice_questions.text: Give two reasons why teenage girls may have higher iron requirements than boys of the same age.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: menstrual blood loss depletes iron stores each month; rapid growth during adolescence increases the demand for iron (for haemoglobin and muscle development); teenage girls are sometimes more likely to have restricted diets that are low in red meat. Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe three adaptations a cook should make when preparing a three-course meal for a guest with coeliac disease.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three distinct, relevant points: replace wheat-based pasta/bread/flour with gluten-free alternatives (rice, gluten-free pasta, gluten-free flour); ensure all equipment and surfaces have been thoroughly cleaned to prevent cross-contamination from gluten-containing foods; check all processed ingredients (sauces, stocks, dressings) for hidden gluten; use gluten-free bread or gluten-free crackers for any starter; choose desserts based on rice, potato starch or gluten-free oats rather than wheat-based pastry or sponge. Up to 3 marks.

practice_questions.text: Oliver is 70 years old, lives alone, and rarely goes outdoors. His doctor has suggested his vitamin D levels may be low. Explain why Oliver is at risk and identify two steps he could take to improve his vitamin D status.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 2 marks per developed point. (1) Risk: vitamin D is synthesised in the skin when it is exposed to sunlight; because Oliver rarely goes outdoors, his skin synthesis will be minimal. This is compounded by the fact that ageing reduces the skin's ability to synthesise vitamin D. Without adequate vitamin D, calcium absorption is impaired, risking bone loss and osteomalacia. (2) Steps: take a vitamin D supplement (Public Health England recommends 10 micrograms per day for all adults, especially those over 65); eat vitamin-D-rich foods such as oily fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines), eggs and fortified cereals or spreads. 1 mark for identifying the mechanism of risk; 1 mark for developed consequence, per point.

practice_questions.text: Describe three ways that planning meals in advance can help a family on a limited budget to eat a balanced diet.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three of: writing a shopping list prevents impulse purchases and reduces overspending; planning uses up all ingredients and reduces food waste; buying seasonal ingredients (e.g. root vegetables in winter) is cheaper; batch cooking and freezing reduces the cost per portion; choosing own-brand or supermarket-own versions of staples (pasta, tinned tomatoes, oats) without reducing nutritional quality. Up to 3 marks.

practice_questions.text: A school canteen is redesigning its menu to better support the nutritional needs of 11- to 16-year-old students. Evaluate the extent to which the canteen should prioritise calcium and vitamin D in its menu planning, using your knowledge of the nutritional needs of this age group.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): Argues both sides with evidence. FOR prioritising calcium and vitamin D: bone density peaks in the early twenties, so the teenage years are a critical window; calcium is needed for bone mineralisation and muscle function; vitamin D is needed for calcium absorption; deficiency during adolescence increases osteoporosis risk in later life; many teenagers eat too little dairy (fear of fat) or have inadequate sun exposure; calcium-rich foods (dairy, fortified plant milks, dark green vegetables) are affordable and easy to include. AGAINST/nuancing: a school canteen cannot address home eating; teenagers also have high needs for iron (especially girls), protein, folate and iodine; a menu solely focused on calcium and vitamin D may neglect variety; individual variation means some students (vegans, lactose intolerant) cannot benefit from dairy-based sources unless alternatives are offered. JUDGEMENT: explicitly stated and supported (e.g. 'Calcium and vitamin D should be a priority, but the canteen should simultaneously address iron for girls and protein variety — a menu-planning checklist rather than a single-nutrient focus would be most effective.'). Accurate use of vitamin D, calcium, peak bone density, osteoporosis, haemoglobin, RNI terminology throughout.

Secure (7–9 marks): Addresses both calcium/vitamin D case AND at least one other competing nutritional priority. Reaches a judgement but the weighing may be partial or the evidence one-sided.

Developing (4–6 marks): Describes calcium and/or vitamin D needs without sustained analysis of both sides; may list foods without explaining the reasoning; judgement weak or absent.

Emerging (1–3 marks): Basic points about teenagers needing calcium with little or no development, application to the canteen context, or judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which ingredient acts as a natural emulsifier in mayonnaise, allowing oil and water to form a stable mixture?
A. Vinegar
B. Mustard
C. Lecithin in egg yolk
D. Salt
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for C. Lecithin in egg yolk.

practice_questions.text: State two ways of preventing enzymic browning in freshly cut apple.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each valid method (any two from): brush or coat with lemon juice (or any acidic liquid); submerge in cold water to restrict oxygen; blanch briefly in boiling water to denature the enzyme; store in an airtight container to reduce oxygen exposure.

practice_questions.text: Describe how yeast acts as a raising agent in bread-making.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: yeast is a biological (living microorganism) raising agent (1); it feeds on sugars in the dough and produces carbon dioxide gas through fermentation (1); the carbon dioxide is trapped by the gluten network in the dough, causing it to rise (prove) before the yeast is killed and the gas expands further during baking (1).

practice_questions.text: Soren is making a Victoria sponge. He creams the butter and sugar for only 30 seconds before adding the other ingredients. His sponge comes out flat and dense. Explain why insufficient creaming affects the final texture of the cake.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: creaming is a mechanical raising method in which the fat (butter) traps air (1); the sharp crystals of the sugar cut tiny pockets into the fat, which the fat holds in place (1); if the butter and sugar are only briefly mixed, fewer air pockets are incorporated (1); in the oven, there is less trapped air to expand and raise the cake, so the sponge is flat, dense and heavy rather than light and airy (1).

practice_questions.text:
A small village bakery sells both choux pastry eclairs and shortcrust pastry tarts. The baker is thinking about which raising agents are responsible for the texture of each product.

Evaluate how the raising agent used in choux pastry compares to the raising agent used in shortcrust pastry, considering the mechanism, the structural requirements and the final textural outcome. Which approach is more suitable for achieving a hollow, airy shell, and why?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): Clear and accurate explanation of steam as the raising agent in choux pastry (water in the mixture converts to steam at 100 degrees C, causing the pastry to expand and create a hollow shell); clear and accurate explanation of mechanical raising in shortcrust pastry (rubbing in and folding incorporate small amounts of air, but shortcrust is not intended to rise significantly); developed comparison of structural requirements (choux needs a high proportion of eggs so the egg protein coagulates quickly, holding the expanded hollow shell; shortcrust relies on fat limiting gluten for a short, crumbly texture rather than a light rise); evaluative weighing of strengths and limitations of each method in achieving an airy hollow shell; explicit supported final judgement that steam is superior for a hollow shell because it is a far more powerful raising force than the air incorporated mechanically into shortcrust; accurate food-science vocabulary throughout (steam, coagulation, gluten, mechanical, aeration).
Secure (7-9 marks): Correct identification of both raising mechanisms; some comparison of structural requirements; judgement present but weighing of evidence is partial or one side is underdeveloped.
Developing (4-6 marks): One raising mechanism well-explained; some comparison with the other; limited evaluation or judgement stated without full support.
Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic relevant points only; may name the correct raising agents without explaining how they work.

practice_questions.text: Name two functional properties of fat and explain how each one is used in making shortcrust pastry.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Accurate identification and explanation of shortening (fat coats gluten strands, preventing them from bonding into a continuous elastic network, producing a crumbly, tender texture) and plasticity (fat remains workable and pliable across temperatures, allowing it to be rubbed evenly into the flour without melting or crumbling); both properties clearly linked to the specific outcome in shortcrust pastry; accurate vocabulary used.
Secure (3-4 marks): Both functional properties named and mostly correctly explained; link to shortcrust pastry present but not fully developed for both.
Developing (2 marks): One property well-explained; the second property named but not clearly linked to shortcrust pastry.
Emerging (1 mark): One property named with minimal or no explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of primary processing?
A. Turning flour into bread dough
B. Converting milk into yoghurt using bacterial cultures
C. Milling harvested wheat grain into flour
D. Cooking fruit with sugar to produce jam
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for C.

practice_questions.text: State two nutrients that are legally required to be added back to white flour during fortification.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of any two from: thiamin (B1); niacin (B3); calcium; iron. Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe how UHT processing of milk differs from pasteurisation and explain one effect this difference has on the milk's nutritional or sensory properties.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for describing the temperature/time difference: UHT heats milk to at least 135°C for 1–2 seconds compared with pasteurisation at 72°C for 15 seconds (1). 1 mark for the consequence: UHT causes greater destruction of heat-sensitive B vitamins (1). 1 mark for the sensory or practical effect: UHT has a slightly cooked or caramelised flavour compared with pasteurised milk, and does not require refrigeration until opened (1). Maximum 3 marks.

practice_questions.text: Tariq is a 45-year-old man who has been told by his GP to reduce his LDL cholesterol. His dietitian suggests switching to a cholesterol-lowering spread. Explain how cholesterol-lowering spreads work and whether they are a reliable solution for Tariq.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Mechanism (2): cholesterol-lowering spreads contain plant sterols or stanols which are structurally similar to cholesterol (1); they compete with dietary cholesterol for absorption in the small intestine, reducing the amount that enters the bloodstream (1). Reliability evaluation (2): evidence supports a reduction in LDL cholesterol of approximately 10–15% with daily consistent use (1); however, the effect requires daily use and the spread is more expensive than standard alternatives, which means Tariq needs to use it every day to see benefit (1). Two developed explanations for full marks.

practice_questions.text: A breakfast cereal manufacturer is updating its product range. One new cereal is fortified with folic acid and iron; another is modified to include added plant sterols. Evaluate the health benefits and limitations of using fortification and modification as strategies to improve public health through food.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12): Distinguishes clearly between fortification (restoring lost/absent nutrients for a population) and modification (adding bioactive compounds to produce a physiological change). Health benefits of fortification developed: folic acid reduces risk of neural tube defects in early pregnancy; iron fortification addresses widespread iron-deficiency anaemia, particularly in young women and adolescents; calcium and B vitamins in flour support bone health and nervous system function across the population. Limitations of fortification: does not help individuals with specific deficiencies needing medical intervention; fortified food still needs to be consumed daily; over-fortification of some nutrients (e.g. fat-soluble vitamins A and D) could cause toxicity if multiple fortified products consumed. Health benefits of modification developed: plant sterols in spreads clinically proven to reduce LDL cholesterol by 10–15% with daily use, supporting cardiovascular health. Limitations of modification: requires daily consistent use; not suitable for pregnant women or children; higher cost limits accessibility; effect on some groups unproven; consumers may over-rely on modified foods rather than broader dietary change. Reaches a supported judgement: fortification is the more reliable public health tool because it benefits the whole population passively (e.g. white flour is in bread eaten daily by most people), whereas modified foods require specific conscious purchasing and daily compliance. Accurate and sustained use of terminology throughout. Judgement explicitly weighs the scale of benefit (whole-population vs individual daily users).

Secure (7–9): Addresses both fortification and modification with developed points for each. Benefits and limitations present for both. Reaches a judgement but the weighing of evidence is partial.

Developing (4–6): Identifies benefits and limitations of one or both strategies with some development. May be one-sided or descriptive. Judgement present but weakly supported.

Emerging (1–3): Basic identification of benefits. Little or no analysis of limitations. No judgement or judgement unsupported. May confuse fortification and modification.

practice_questions.text: Give one example of secondary processing that uses milk as its primary processed starting ingredient.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one correct example of secondary processing using milk: yoghurt; cheese (any variety); butter; cream; ice cream. Answer must name a product made from milk, not just describe a process.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following must be included on a pre-packed food label by law?
A) Serving suggestions
B) Country of origin for all ingredients
C) The net quantity (weight or volume) of the food
D) A photograph of the dish
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for C.

practice_questions.text: State what the term 'Reference Intake (RI)' means on a food label.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: the guideline daily amount for a specific nutrient or energy; 1 mark for: based on an average adult consuming 2,000 kcal per day. Accept equivalent wording.

practice_questions.text: Describe how traffic-light labelling helps a consumer compare two breakfast cereals in a supermarket.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: traffic-light labelling uses colour-coded icons (red, amber, green) for fat, saturated fat, sugars and salt (1); red indicates a high amount per 100 g, green indicates a low amount (1); the consumer can quickly see which cereal has fewer red or amber ratings and therefore which is a lower-fat or lower-sugar choice without having to interpret numerical values (1).

practice_questions.text: A supermarket places a multi-pack of sugary cereal bars at child eye-height near the checkout, reduces the price by 50% and labels the shelf 'special offer'. Explain two ways in which this marketing strategy could influence the food choices of families shopping with children.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks per strategy (2 required). Strategy 1: point-of-sale placement at child eye-height near the checkout deliberately targets children who are waiting and more likely to ask for impulse purchases (1); because children see the product repeatedly at a familiar location, this means parents experience pester power and may buy foods they would otherwise have passed by (1). Strategy 2: the 50% price reduction makes the product appear highly cost-effective (1); because families on a budget are sensitive to price, the reduced cost overrides the nutritional consideration and they may buy a larger quantity than they need, consuming more sugary product over the following week (1).

practice_questions.text: A secondary school is reviewing the nutritional information on the meals it serves in its canteen. The canteen manager wants to introduce traffic-light labelling on every dish. Explain the benefits and limitations of using traffic-light labelling to help students make healthier food choices at lunchtime.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): explains clearly how traffic lights work (colour-coding fat, saturates, sugars and salt using per 100 g thresholds) and why this benefits students (quick visual scan without numerical literacy; helps identify lower-fat or lower-sugar options at a glance; raises awareness of less obvious nutrients such as salt). Then explains at least two limitations: students may select green-labelled items that don't meet their total energy needs (a green-labelled salad may not be enough for an active teenager); traffic lights reflect per 100 g figures not per portion, so a small high-sugar item may show as amber when the portion eaten is large; marketing and peer pressure may override label information; students may not understand the system. Two or three well-developed chains of reasoning.

Secure (3–4): explains benefits and at least one limitation with some development and application to the school context.

Developing (1–2): states benefits or limitations with minimal development; limited application to the scenario.

Emerging (0): superficial response with no developed reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how food marketing strategies such as buy one get one free offers, meal deals and media advertising can influence food choice, and consider whether food labelling provides an effective counterbalance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9): breaks marketing into distinct components and examines how each works: BOGOF — drives bulk purchases of specific products (often high in fat/sugar/salt), meaning consumers spend more than planned and may overconsume the promoted food; the financial saving feels rational but the nutritional outcome may be negative (2). Meal deals — structure the choice away from open selection toward a fixed combination; the drink component is frequently a sugary drink, meaning consumers accept a less healthy drink because it is included in a perceived value package (2). Media and advertising — repetition creates brand preference and desire independent of nutritional merit; children particularly vulnerable (1). Analyses whether labelling counterbalances: traffic-light labelling can inform aware consumers but is voluntary; mandatory nutrition declaration provides information but requires numerical literacy; marketing operates on emotion and habit rather than information, meaning labelling may fail to counteract impulse purchasing; some consumers actively use labels, especially post-health scare or diagnosis. Examines the interaction between marketing and labelling: a product with red traffic lights but a compelling BOGOF offer may still sell strongly, demonstrating that marketing often overrides information. Sustained analysis throughout with accurate terminology.

Secure (5–7): analyses at least two marketing strategies with reasonable development; some analysis of labelling as counterbalance; mostly accurate.

Developing (2–4): describes marketing strategies with limited analysis; limited engagement with labelling.

Emerging (1): brief and mainly descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Identify the type of sensory test in which a taster is given three samples, two identical and one different, and must identify which is the odd one out.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: triangle test.

practice_questions.text: State the three pillars included in the precise definition of 'cuisine'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each: distinctive ingredients (1); specific preparation and cooking methods or equipment (1); presentation or serving techniques (1). All three required for full marks.

practice_questions.text: State two controlled conditions that must be in place when running a taste panel for sensory evaluation.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of any two valid conditions: samples served at the same temperature; samples given neutral coded labels (e.g. three-digit numbers, not A/B); tasters separated by partitions to prevent influence; water and plain crackers provided between samples to clear the palate; room free of strong odours; tasters neither hungry nor full; panel large enough (10-20 people minimum) for statistical reliability. Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Freya is a food technology student developing a new reduced-salt tomato soup. She wants to know whether the change in salt content is detectable by tasters. Explain which sensory test she should use and describe how she would set it up.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for identifying and justifying the triangle test: Freya should use a triangle test (1) because it is a discrimination test designed to detect whether tasters can tell the difference between two similar products — in this case the original and reduced-salt versions (1). Up to 2 marks for describing the set-up: three coded samples presented (two of one version, one of the other, in random order) (1); tasters work in isolation with a palate cleanser between samples; they must identify the odd one out; if most tasters cannot correctly identify the different sample, the reformulation has been successful (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe the key features of one international cuisine of your choice, using the three-pillar definition of cuisine throughout your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Marking is by structure, not by choice of cuisine. 1 mark for each pillar correctly applied to the named cuisine: distinctive ingredients accurately described for the chosen cuisine (1); specific preparation or cooking method or equipment accurately described (1); presentation or eating pattern accurately described (1). Accept any accurate cuisine description (Italian, Indian, Japanese, Mexican, West African, Chinese, etc.) as long as all three pillars are covered.

practice_questions.text: A small artisan bakery is developing two new sourdough bread recipes and wants to choose between them using sensory evaluation. Evaluate the sensory testing methods they could use, and recommend which combination of tests would give them the most useful information about both consumer preference and the sensory profile of each loaf.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12): evaluates preference tests (paired preference — straightforward but tells only which is preferred overall, not why; hedonic scale — more nuanced, tells how strongly each loaf is liked or disliked, giving a numeric dataset); evaluates discrimination tests (triangle test — could check whether tasters detect meaningful differences in crumb texture or crust, useful for quality consistency but does not measure preference); evaluates grading tests (ranking — quick and simple for ordering two loaves by a single attribute; rating — gives a score per attribute; profiling — most information-rich, builds a full sensory picture of each loaf across multiple attributes such as crust colour, crumb texture, sourness, aroma, saltiness, chew). Reaches a supported judgement: a combination of paired preference (to confirm which loaf consumers prefer overall) and profiling (to understand the specific sensory attributes driving that preference, enabling the baker to refine the recipe) would give the most complete picture; this is better than any single test because it captures both emotional response and analytical detail. Uses precise vocabulary (controlled conditions, coded samples, palate cleanser, taste panel size, olfactory, taste receptors). Applied throughout to the bakery scenario.

Secure (7–9): evaluates at least two test types with reasonable development; reaches a partial judgement; mostly accurate and applied to the scenario.

Developing (4–6): describes tests with limited evaluation; one-sided or descriptive; partial application to the bakery context.

Emerging (1–3): names some tests with no evaluation; no supported judgement.

practice_questions.text:
What does PAL stand for?
A. Physical Activity Level
B. Protein Absorption Limit
C. Personal Allowance Index
D. Physical Analysis Limit
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for A (Physical Activity Level).

practice_questions.text: State the recommended percentage of total energy that should come from fat in a balanced diet.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: 35% or less (accept 'no more than 35%').

practice_questions.text: A recipe uses 200 g of cheddar cheese. A food table shows that cheddar provides 1.6 g of calcium per 100 g. Calculate the total calcium provided by the cheese in this recipe. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct method: (200 ÷ 100) × 1.6 = 2 × 1.6; 1 mark for correct answer: 3.2 g of calcium. Accept the answer with or without the unit if the working clearly shows it.

practice_questions.text: Describe three factors that affect a person's basal metabolic rate (BMR).
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three distinct, correctly described factors: age (BMR decreases with age as muscle mass declines and metabolism slows); gender (males typically have a higher BMR because of greater muscle mass); body composition/muscle mass (more muscle tissue means a higher BMR because muscle burns more energy at rest than fat tissue); hormones (e.g. an overactive thyroid raises BMR); life stage/pregnancy (BMR increases during pregnancy). Up to 3 marks.

practice_questions.text: Jabir is a 17-year-old who plays football twice a week and cycles to college every day. He is trying to understand why he needs more energy than his 17-year-old cousin who works from home and rarely exercises. Explain how BMR and PAL together determine Jabir's higher energy requirement.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 2 marks per developed explanation. (1) BMR: even at rest, Jabir may have a higher BMR than his cousin because regular exercise builds lean muscle mass; muscle burns more energy at rest than fat, so his resting metabolic rate is elevated (1 mark point; 1 mark reason/consequence). (2) PAL: Jabir's daily cycling and football sessions mean his PAL multiplier is significantly higher (1.7 or above vs a sedentary 1.4); because total energy = BMR × PAL, even a modest difference in PAL compounds to a large difference in total daily requirement (1 mark point; 1 mark development using the formula). 1 mark for identification; 1 mark for developed reasoning, per point.

practice_questions.text: Nadia is planning to modify a beef lasagne recipe to reduce its saturated fat content while keeping it nutritionally balanced. She carries out a nutritional analysis and finds that one portion provides 22 g of saturated fat, which exceeds the recommended daily maximum of 20 g. Evaluate two modifications Nadia could make to reduce the saturated fat content, considering both the nutritional impact and the effect on the sensory properties of the finished dish.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): Identifies two well-chosen modifications (e.g. 1: swap beef mince for extra-lean mince or substitute half with lentils/TVP; 2: replace full-fat creme fraiche or cheese topping with a lower-fat bechamel using semi-skimmed milk and a reduced amount of cheddar, or use a ricotta-based layer). For each modification, analyses both the nutritional impact (quantitative or descriptive: how much saturated fat is saved; which other nutrients are affected positively or negatively) AND the sensory effect (texture, flavour, appearance — e.g. removing full-fat cheese reduces the creamy, rich mouthfeel and golden top; lentils add a slightly earthy flavour and denser texture). Accurate use of saturated fat, BMI, energy density, palatability and reference intake vocabulary. Analysis is not merely descriptive but examines relationships and consequences.

Secure (5–7 marks): Identifies two modifications with reasonable development of either nutritional or sensory impact (not necessarily both for each). Mostly accurate. Some analysis of relationships.

Developing (3–4 marks): Identifies modifications but gives only descriptive rather than analytical treatment. Little examination of sensory consequences or the interplay between fat reduction and palatability.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Names a modification (e.g. 'use less cheese') with no analysis of the nutritional or sensory consequences.

practice_questions.text:
Which condition is caused by a long-term deficiency of both vitamin D and calcium in children?
A. Iron-deficiency anaemia
B. Rickets
C. Type 2 diabetes
D. Dental caries
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for B (Rickets).

practice_questions.text: State two dietary changes a person with high blood pressure could make to lower their risk.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: reduce salt/sodium intake; reduce saturated fat intake; increase fruit and vegetable intake; increase dietary fibre; reduce alcohol intake; eat oily fish for omega-3 fatty acids; use herbs and spices instead of salt when cooking. Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a diet high in free sugars can lead to dental decay.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three accurate, distinct points: bacteria in the mouth ferment free sugars; this produces acids; the acids dissolve (demineralise) tooth enamel; frequent consumption (especially between meals) means teeth are repeatedly exposed to acid attacks; the protective effect of saliva is reduced between meals; over time, holes (cavities/dental caries) form in the enamel. Up to 3 marks.

practice_questions.text: Fatima is a 17-year-old vegetarian who is often tired, has pale skin and struggles to concentrate at school. Her GP suspects iron-deficiency anaemia. Explain why Fatima may be at risk and identify two dietary strategies that could help.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 2 marks per developed explanation. (1) Risk: Fatima follows a vegetarian diet, which typically provides only non-haem iron from plant sources (lentils, spinach, fortified cereals) rather than the more easily absorbed haem iron from red meat; non-haem iron has lower bioavailability, meaning her body absorbs a smaller proportion of the iron she eats; she may also have higher iron needs because of menstrual losses. (2) Strategies: eat iron-rich plant foods (fortified cereals, dark green vegetables, lentils, beans) alongside a source of vitamin C (orange juice, fresh tomatoes, peppers), because vitamin C converts non-haem iron into a more readily absorbed form; avoid drinking tea or coffee with meals, as tannins inhibit iron absorption. 1 mark for identification of risk mechanism; 1 mark for developed consequence or specific strategy per point.

practice_questions.text: Describe the main dietary risk factors for developing type 2 diabetes.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three accurate points: high intake of refined carbohydrates and/or free sugars (causing repeated blood glucose spikes and high insulin demand, leading to insulin resistance over time); obesity or excess body fat (especially abdominal fat is strongly linked to insulin resistance); low dietary fibre intake (fibre slows glucose absorption and helps regulate blood glucose levels); large portion sizes and a high-calorie diet that promotes weight gain. Up to 3 marks.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the dietary changes a person newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes should make to manage their condition, considering both short-term blood glucose control and long-term health outcomes.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): Evaluates dietary changes under at least two dimensions (short-term BG control AND long-term outcomes), using specific, accurate dietary advice and linking it to the underlying mechanisms. Short-term: reducing free sugars and refined carbohydrates reduces blood glucose spikes and lowers the demand on the pancreas to release insulin, helping to prevent hyperglycaemia; increasing dietary fibre (wholegrain bread, oats, pulses) slows glucose absorption so the rise in blood glucose after meals is gentler. Long-term: managing body weight through calorie reduction and increased fibre intake improves insulin sensitivity, which is the central problem in type 2 diabetes; reducing saturated fat lowers CHD risk (people with type 2 diabetes are at higher risk of cardiovascular disease); adequate calcium and vitamin D protect bones (some diabetes medications can affect bone density). JUDGEMENT: explicitly weighs the relative importance of changes (e.g. 'Reducing free sugars and losing weight are the highest-priority changes because they directly address insulin resistance — the root cause — whereas fat and micronutrient management, while valuable, address secondary complications.'). Accurate use of insulin resistance, blood glucose, glycaemic index, dietary fibre, LDL cholesterol and atherosclerosis throughout.

Secure (7–9 marks): Addresses both short-term glucose control and at least one long-term consideration. Reaches a partial judgement. Mostly accurate, with some applied vocabulary.

Developing (4–6 marks): Describes dietary changes without sustained evaluation of both time horizons; judgement weak or absent; one-sided or mainly descriptive.

Emerging (1–3 marks): Basic points about eating less sugar with no development of mechanism, application to the person, or comparison of the importance of different changes.
